proposed_edges.relationship: In Donald Wright’s Dictionary of Canadian Biography entry on Creighton (2013), Miller recalls Creighton’s doctoral supervision as prompt and collegial, with suggestions offered as advice rather than instructions.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Read the paragraph beginning “Many of those welcomed into his home were former students” in Wright’s Dictionary of Canadian Biography article (2013). Wright names Miller among Creighton’s doctoral students and quotes Miller’s recollection: “these are suggestions, not instructions”. This is Miller’s testimony as quoted by Wright; the underlying interview and dissertation were not read. 2013 dates the published recollection, not the supervision. No transmission of Creighton’s nationalism or Laurentian interpretation is claimed.

proposed_edges.relationship: Coulthard’s Subjects of Empire? (2009) recommends Miller’s Shingwauk’s Vision (1996) as an authority for the history of residential schools while describing exclusion and assimilation before the turn to recognition politics.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Fresh reading of the University of Victoria repository dissertation: printed p. 5 (PDF p. 13), surrounding argument and nn. 13–15; bibliography printed pp. 232–233 (PDF pp. 240–241). Coulthard discusses repressive state power before the 1969 White Paper, including residential schools; n. 15 recommends Miller’s 1996 book as an “authoritative account”. Note 14 cites John Tobias’s chapter in Miller’s edited Sweet Promises, so that separate argument is not attributed to Miller. Coulthard misstates the book’s subtitle as A History of Indian Residential Schools; the title is A History of Native Residential Schools. This is a named historical authority within Coulthard’s argument, not evidence that he adopted Miller’s whole interpretation, criticized Miller, or derived his theory of recognition from him. The 2014 book and Miller’s book remain unread.

proposed_edges.relationship: Trevithick’s 1998 review identifies Miller’s “Reading Photographs, Reading Voices” (1996) as a methodological case for supplementing documentary records with photographs, literature and especially oral history to recover students’ experiences of residential schooling.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Read Scott Trevithick, “Native Residential Schooling in Canada: A Review of Literature” (1998), printed pp. 58–59, with title/issue page and bibliography p. 85, from the institutional I-Portal PDF. On p. 58 Trevithick explains that conventional documentary sources are insufficient for reconstructing students’ experiences and names “pictures, literature, and especially oral history” as Miller’s alternatives. On p. 59 he identifies their use in Shingwauk’s Vision. Bibliography p. 85 dates both works 1996; the later essay collection of 2004 is not their original publication. This is Trevithick’s substantive reading, not a fresh reading of Miller’s chapter or book. It establishes a particular methodological contribution, not priority, universal success, community endorsement, or a general claim about the reliability of oral testimony. No testimony is reproduced. Existing edge_2828 concerns the national synthesis and edge_2829 concerns responsibility; neither has the oral-history endpoint.
